sections.overview: Meyer’s goshawk is a large forest raptor of the Moluccas, New Guinea, the Bismarck Archipelago and the Solomon Islands. It was traditionally placed in Accipiter; some modern bird checklists use Astur meyerianus. Adults show a bold black-and-white pattern, while juveniles are browner and less sharply marked. It is secretive and seldom observed, so many details of its ecology remain based on scattered records.
sections.identification: The adult has dark slate to black upperparts, white underparts finely barred grey-brown, a dark barred tail and red eyes; the cere and legs are yellowish. A rare dark morph has much darker underparts. Juveniles are brown above with buff-edged feathers and heavier streaking below. Standard reference works give a total length of about 43–53 cm and a wingspan of 86–105 cm. Published mass figures are sparse: one reported adult male weighed about 530 g and one female about 1,100 g, illustrating pronounced female-biased size dimorphism but not defining population averages. No dependable body height or width range was found. Its large size, strongly barred pale underside and broad goshawk-like build help distinguish it from smaller island accipiters; check plumage age and locality as well.
sections.habitat: It inhabits lowland, hill and montane forest, including forest edges and nearby wooded gardens. Its island range extends from the Moluccas east through New Guinea and the Bismarck group to the Solomon Islands. It has been recorded from low elevations up to around 1,800 m in some species references; local occurrence and elevation vary between islands. Forest loss is a concern in parts of this range.
sections.diet: It is a carnivorous hunter that takes birds and lizards; small mammals are also considered probable prey. Reports suggest it may pursue pigeons and other birds with a fast low flight through or beside forest. Direct diet studies and prey-frequency data are limited, so a detailed menu cannot be quantified confidently.
sections.behavior: Meyer’s goshawk is diurnal and generally difficult to see in dense forest. It hunts from cover or a perch and can make a rapid attack on prey. Available records are too sparse to establish regular movements, social organization or a detailed daily activity pattern. Its conspicuous calls and behavior are not well documented in field sources reviewed.
sections.reproduction: The species nests in forest, but published accounts provide little dependable detail on nest structure, clutch size, incubation or breeding season across its range. As with other raptors, the female is larger, but that size difference should not be used alone to sex birds in the field. More island-specific breeding observations are needed.
sections.ecology: As a forest predator, it occupies the upper levels of island food webs and may regulate populations of medium-sized birds and other vertebrates. Its secretive nature and low encounter rates make population estimates difficult. Habitat quality and the continuity of forest are likely important, but the exact response of local populations to forest change is not well quantified.
sections.conservation: The 2016 IUCN Red List assessment classified the species as Least Concern, citing its broad island range, while also reporting a decreasing population trend and ongoing habitat loss. That assessment is not the latest; status should be checked against the current IUCN record before being treated as current. A broad range does not mean every island population is secure, especially where forest is being cleared.
